summary.prose: s2 puts a router in front of every request and moves admin work and indexing work off the main thread. Admin methods (daemon.status, debug-status, repo.list, the TUI's config and guide reads, shutdown and update) run on an admin worker that answers from the status board; code indexing, the file watcher and every indexing method run on a code-indexing worker, and document summaries execute on a document-summary worker that still starts a summary only while code indexing is idle. Session methods keep running on the main thread as today until s3, reaching the indexing workers through a small cross-thread port. Graph compaction becomes idle maintenance: after 30 quiet minutes, when enough space is reclaimable, the daemon holds every request except daemon.status, compacts, and resumes.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Alternative a1: a routing main thread plus worker threads by class of work. The main thread owns the Unix socket, framing and the attached-client registry, and does no handler work. Each request is classified (admin, session or indexing) and forwarded over a thread channel to its target: the admin worker, the code-indexing worker, or the session's pooled worker (session id = the request's client label and process id). Workers each load the handler runtime and open their own store handles under a verified per-store threading policy: direct use where a store is proven safe, a shared semaphore with guaranteed release where it is not. MCP step state (the four step state stores) moves into a store shared by all threads, so it outlives any worker; a detached workflow run stays owned by the worker that started it, which is not released while the run is active, and the run's record is published where every thread can read it. A request that carries no valid client identity is served on one shared unattributed worker, as today's daemon serves it, kept apart from every session. A shared status board lets every thread publish what it is doing, which the admin worker reads for daemon status and liveness.

ownedContracts.name: Method-class registry
ownedContracts.purpose: Declares the class of every RPC and stream method the daemon serves, so the router sends each request to the right kind of thread and no method is left unclassified.

consumedContracts.name: Store guard and per-store threading policy
consumedContracts.purpose: Lets any thread use a store safely: records, per store, whether it is used directly or through a semaphore, and gives one helper that acquires and always releases the store's semaphore. Waiting for a lock is always asynchronous, so a waiting thread keeps serving its other work.

consumedContracts.name: Thread channel and target registry
consumedContracts.purpose: The one message contract between the router and every worker: request, reply, stream frame, cancel and error envelopes, plus the registry where a worker registers as the target for a class of work. A session-class request with no valid session id resolves to the unattributed target.

consumedContracts.name: Thread status board
consumedContracts.purpose: Shared record each thread updates as it starts and finishes work: the router publishes its attached-client snapshot, the indexing workers publish lane state, summary-sweep progress, each repository's completeness and the unattributed-entity count, and detached workflow runs publish their full poll state, so the admin thread can answer status, debug-status, liveness and run polls without calling into a busy thread or touching a store.

boundary.internal: The main-thread router (connection handling, classification through the method-class registry, envelope forwarding to registered targets, writing replies and frames back, observing worker exits and reclaiming a dead worker's store locks), the admin worker, and indexing on two workers: the code-indexing worker hosting the index queue's code lane and the file-watcher feed and serving every indexing-class method, and the document-summary worker running the summary lane, starting a summary only while code indexing is idle. Both indexing workers publish lane state, idleness, summary-sweep progress, the full registered-repository records with each repository's completeness, and the unattributed-entity count with its reasons on the status board after every change. Session-class methods keep running on the main thread exactly as today until s3 moves them; there is no fallback worker. Shutdown and the locks-lost path keep today's behaviour with the workers included (each stops its work, the queue drains, the main thread closes the stores after the workers exit). Validation: ac1 — daemon.status and the TUI's admin reads answer within 100 ms while an indexing pass runs and another worker keeps an LMDB write transaction open; ac2 — each admin method's response matches today's recorded response; ac3 — a test enumerates every served RPC and stream method and fails on any without a class, and dispatch tests assert admin methods ran on the admin thread and indexing methods on the code-indexing thread; ac4/ac5 — a session request is answered during an indexing pass, and a file change is indexed while a session request runs; ac6 — summaries start only while code indexing is idle, and lane order and indexed results equal the single-thread baseline; ac7 — queue status and idle waiting read from another thread reflect the indexing workers' real state. Also: debug-status keeps every field including lastMethod; daemon.status and repo.list read only the status board and keep today's full response shapes. Also maintenance compaction: idle detection (30 min, configurable), the reclaimable-space threshold (25% and 256 MB), maintenance mode holding every request except daemon.status, workers closing and reopening their graph handles around the main thread's compaction, and the manual daemon.compact keeping today's responses. s2 adds the additive sc4 method publishLane and its hub binding.

adjacentBoundaries.internal: Verifying each store from several threads of one process (the LMDB graph environment, every Lance table, the in-memory DuckDB pool), including that a worker opening and later releasing its handles does not close a descriptor the process's locks depend on; the semaphore implementation over process-wide shared memory and its holder record; moving the four in-memory step state stores onto the shared step-state store with today's TTL; the status board's attached-client, sweep-progress and run-record slots; the thread channel's serialisation and the target registry's bookkeeping; the status board's hub-served layout on the main thread. As the root Story it owns every cross-cutting contract the other Stories consume. Validation: ac1 — one thread writes a repo's entities while another reads the same graph, the reader sees only whole transactions, and an entity's vectors are written only after its graph commit; ac2 — two threads write different artifacts or config entries and a third thread reads both back; ac3 — no code path outside the daemon opens a store; ac4 — a throwing LMDB transaction on one thread leaves nothing visible to another. Also: a worker opening and releasing its handles keeps the process's LMDB locks; the guard releases on success, throw, cancel and worker kill; an acquisition past its limit fails; nested acquisition is refused. Step-state compatibility: for each of the four kinds, token rotation (analyze, workflow), stable-token update (review) or consume-and-mint per stage (code-review, where a superseded token fails), read refresh of expiry, the 100-entry eviction and a missing-token error behave as today. LMDB is opened once per process and never closed by a worker; lock reclaim waits for a dead worker's in-flight native calls. Per store, a quiescence observation with a time limit and an unhealthy-store outcome when it is exceeded; a guard wait never blocks its thread.

The session pool, moving every session-class method off the main thread: session-id mapping, per-session FIFO, worker creation and idle release, containment of a failing worker (its in-flight requests fail with an error, the next request gets a new worker), routing each step handler's state through the shared step-state store, the unattributed worker, inline nested calls, and ownership of detached workflow runs (records on the status board, abort routed to the owner, failure on owner exit, never idle-released while a run is active). Validation: ac1 — session B is answered while session A's worker spins; ac2 — A's second request starts only after its first completes; ac3 — requests from one client process over separate connections run on one worker, released after the idle timeout; ac4 — a worker failure fails only its session's requests; ac5 — provider calls stay serial (no Promise.all reaching a provider); ac6 — a step token minted before an idle release resumes on the new worker; ac7 — ping and daemon.status answer within 100 ms while a session worker spins the CPU for minutes. Also: unattributed requests are served apart from sessions; a nested in-daemon call completes without deadlock; a detached run survives idle time, accepts an abort from another thread, and is marked failed when its owner exits; a poll from another thread, and after the owner has gone, returns the same frames-since-cursor, model, result and error as today. The board's forgetRun operation (an additive sc4 method) is added with the detached-run move, called by the run owner's retention. Session workers take part in maintenance compaction's pause.

The main thread becomes the controller: it loads no handler runtime and runs no request handler, only the socket, classification, forwarding, worker supervision (admin, both indexing workers, the session pool's workers and the unattributed worker: in-flight requests failed, store locks reclaimed, the worker replaced) and shutdown coordination, including the locks-lost path. It also adds a `threads` section to daemon.status and daemon.debug-status from the status board and session pool (additive fields only) and makes the liveness answer report a busy session as busy rather than as a failure. Validation: ac1 — no request handler runs on the main thread; ac2 — a failing worker of any class fails only its own in-flight requests and is replaced; ac3 — shutdown and the locks-lost path behave as today; ac4 — daemon.status lists each thread with class, session, busy state, method and elapsed time; ac5 — with a session worker busy for minutes the liveness answer reports the daemon alive and the session busy; ac6 — every field of today's daemon.status and daemon.debug-status, including clients and sweep progress, is present with the same meaning.

hldContextSlice.rolloutPhase: Phase B — router, admin worker and indexing workers

nonFunctional.performance: Ping and daemon.status answer within 100 ms at the 99th percentile while a session worker is CPU-bound and while an indexing pass runs; routing adds no more than 5 ms per request and per stream frame. A session worker's idle timeout defaults to 15 minutes and is configurable; step state keeps its own 1-hour TTL independent of worker release.
nonFunctional.security: No new listener or socket: the main thread keeps the existing Unix socket and its permissions; shared memory and thread channels are internal to the daemon process; clients still reach the stores only through IPC.
nonFunctional.observability: Every log line carries its thread id and class, and the session id for session work; daemon.status lists every thread with class, session, busy state, current method and elapsed time; a store-lock wait beyond its acquisition limit and a reclaimed lock after a worker exit are logged as warnings.
nonFunctional.durability: Step state survives a worker's release or failure because it lives in the shared step-state store; a detached workflow run lives in its owning worker, which is not released while the run is active, and is marked failed if that worker exits; its poll state lives in shared run storage, so polls still answer after the owner has gone. A worker that exits while holding a store lock has the lock reclaimed by the router. Atomicity is unchanged from today: each LMDB write transaction commits all or nothing, and an operation that writes LMDB then Lance keeps today's order and re-embed recovery. The process's one native LMDB environment is opened by the main thread at start and closed by it at shutdown; each worker opens and may close its own handle on it, which s1 verified keeps the process's locks; a lock held by a dead worker is reclaimed only after its in-flight native calls have finished.

api.name: IpcServer
api.signature: class IpcServer { constructor(forward: (request: RequestEnvelope, deliver: (envelope: ReplyEnvelope | FrameEnvelope) => void) => (() => void), now?: () => number, socketPath?: string); listen(): Promise<void>; close(): Promise<void>; attachedClients(): AttachedClient[]; flushPendingWrites(timeoutMs?: number): Promise<boolean>; disconnectClients(): void }

parameters.name: forward
parameters.type: (request: RequestEnvelope, deliver: (envelope: ReplyEnvelope | FrameEnvelope) => void) => (() => void)
parameters.purpose: Hands one parsed request (with its requestId and the SessionId from the validated client envelope) to the router; deliver writes each reply or frame to the request's socket in today's wire shape; the returned function is called when the socket closes: for a stream it sends a CancelEnvelope (today's abort), for a unary request it only marks the reply to be dropped.

parameters.name: now
parameters.purpose: Clock for connectedAt.

parameters.name: socketPath
parameters.purpose: Socket path, PATHS.sockFile by default.

returns.meaning: The socket server without handler tables: framing, the attached-client registry, today's reply writing.

errors.condition: A line that does not parse is answered {id: -1, error: 'invalid JSON'}, as today.

preconditions: Construction sites move to a forward function: src/daemon/index.ts:1997 (the router) and the tests and helpers that build a server with their own handler tables (including src/db/graph/__tests__/helpers/store-child.ts:178 and :212), which pass directDispatch(rpcHandlers, streamHandlers), an in-thread forward with today's dispatch rules (unknown method by table lookup, stream-to-unary fallback, failureMessage, abort on cancel).
postconditions: new IpcServer(directDispatch(rpc, stream)) behaves on the wire exactly as today's new IpcServer(rpc, stream).

The registry is republished through StatusBoard.publishClients on connect, on close, and after every message updates it (lastMethod, label, pid), before the request is forwarded, so debug-status reports the caller's own 'daemon.debug-status' as its lastMethod exactly as today.

Before running any top-level request other than daemon.status and daemon.compact, its entry point (the router for main-thread session work, the worker's request entry otherwise) requests the daemon maintenance lock shared with ifAvailable and holds it until the request finishes; when it is unavailable the request is answered at once {id, error: "daemon busy: <activity> since <time> (<reason>); retry later"} built from the blocking holder's metadata, and nothing runs. Nested in-daemon calls and cross-class channel calls made under that hold do not request it again. daemon.compact is exempt because it triggers maintenance itself; every other method, daemon.shutdown included, is refused during maintenance (a SIGTERM shutdown waits for the compaction or the hard-exit backstop).

A cross-class request made by a handler that already holds the maintenance lock (a nested in-daemon call routed to another worker) carries underHold: true on its RequestEnvelope, an additive optional field on s1's sc3 envelope delivered by s2; the receiving worker's entry skips the maintenance check for it, so a pending exclusive cannot refuse a request half-way through.

api.name: compactGraphStore

parameters.name: opts
parameters.purpose: A pre-rename check run after the close and before the rename: maintenance passes one that confirms the native environment really closed (no other handle open). When it resolves false, compactGraphStore removes the compacted copy, reopens the original store and rejects with LmdbStoreError('compact: the environment was still open; nothing renamed'), never touching graph.lmdb or its lock file.

errors.condition: As today (store not open, rename or close failure).

preconditions: Called only by the main thread's maintenance while the main thread holds the daemon maintenance lock exclusively (every other request is refused and none is running), after every thread that may hold a graph handle (the admin worker, the code-indexing worker, the document-summary worker and the main thread's own session work) has acknowledged that it has no store work in flight and has closed its handle with closeGraphStore.

Closing a worker's handle is within s1's contract: s1 verified that a worker's open, use, close and exit keep the process's LMDB locks (src/db/graph/__tests__/worker-thread-lock.test.ts), and the approved HLD's Stores section states a worker closing its handle is safe. lmdb-js shares one native environment per process and closes it only when its last handle closes, so the main thread's close inside compactGraphStore ends the environment only because every other handle is already closed; the rename and lock-file removal therefore never run under a handle that is still open.
Change site: src/db/graph/store.ts:861-875 gains the optional beforeRename hook between root.close() and renameSync; without the hook (today's callers) behaviour is unchanged.

The 'environment really closed' check maintenance passes as beforeRename is concrete: every live worker the router supervises has acknowledged a 'graph.close' message only after its own closeGraphStore() resolved (its module instance holds no handle), the main thread's own handle closed inside compactGraphStore, and no worker was started since the acknowledgements were collected; a missing acknowledgement makes the check return false.
postconditions: Every thread reopens its handle lazily on next use after resume, onto the compacted file; no write is lost because nothing writes between the copy and the close.

The document-summary worker reads them for isIndexIdle/isStopping and waits on the code-busy word for waitForIndexIdle, so the summary yield works across threads without a request.

dataModelChanges.entity: Router daemon.info hub op and maintenance state
dataModelChanges.details: A main-thread hub service returning {startedAt, modelState, installedCommit, lmdbFileSizeMb, maintenance?}. bootstrapEmbeddingModel runs once on the main thread (src/daemon/lifecycle.ts:87-109); its decided backend is pushed to every worker ('embedder.backend') because the embedder's activeBackend is per isolate (src/indexer/embedder.ts:85-103). maintenance is {state: 'compacting', since, activity, reason}, read from the maintenance lock's holder metadata (LockManager.query) while the lock is held exclusively; DaemonStatus gains it as an additive optional field.

On the main thread, coordinated through the daemon maintenance lock (lock framework afcfa027, docs/standalone/add-cross-thread-named-lock-framework-E20261022afcfa027/S001/LLD.md). Every request other than daemon.status makes a no-wait shared request (ifAvailable) on the lock 'daemon.maintenance' before it runs, on whichever thread serves it, and holds it until it finishes; indexing jobs take it shared per job and wait (a bounded wait) rather than fail. Idle: no non-admin request has arrived and none is in flight for idleMs (config, default 30 minutes), and the board shows both lanes idle; admin requests (status polls) do not count as activity. Worth it: reclaimable = file size - pages in use * pageSize, pages in use summed from getStats() (branch + leaf + overflow pages) over every named database of the GraphStore (src/db/graph/store.ts:250-312); compaction runs only when reclaimable >= 25% of the file and >= 256 MB (config). Sequence: request the lock exclusively with metadata {activity: 'compaction', reason: '<idle time>, <reclaimable %> / <reclaimable MB> reclaimable'} and timeoutMs = the pause limit (10 minutes, config); by writer preference every new request is refused from that moment with the activity, reason and start time; requests already running finish and release; once granted, tell every live worker to close its graph handle and wait for each acknowledgement; compactGraphStore on the main thread with its pre-rename check; release the lock. Each decision (pause wait, idle time, reclaimable % and bytes, outcome) is logged. Manual daemon.compact on the code-indexing worker keeps today's busy refusal (queue.depth > 0 or processing) and otherwise asks the main thread to run maintenance now and returns its CompactResult; it does not take a shared hold itself, so it cannot block its own maintenance. Non-request store users take the lock too: the prune timer and todo-retention timer on the main thread (src/daemon/index.ts:2014, src/daemon/todos-rpc.ts:1206), the watcher path and every indexing job request it shared with a bounded wait around each run, so none writes during compaction. As a second guard, while maintenance compacts, getGraphStore on any thread other than the compactor rejects with a named MaintenanceInProgress error instead of reopening the store. Long-lived subscription streams (understanding.watch, src/daemon/understanding-rpc.ts:106-113; todos.subscribe) do not hold the lock for their lifetime and do not count as activity for idle detection: each refresh or push takes it shared with ifAvailable and is skipped while maintenance holds it. Bounded streams (workflow.run, codeReview.run, step.call, analyze.run.start, ollama.pull, workflow.review) hold it for their run like any request.

The construction of rpcHandlers/streamHandlers, the understanding routes, the registries and validations moves from main() into a runtime function taking its indexing dependencies: the main thread passes the indexing port; the code-indexing worker passes the real IndexQueue/IndexerService/Watcher. Handler bodies are unchanged. The admin worker runs only the admin module.

The router forwards admin and indexing requests as RequestEnvelopes to the registered admin and code-indexing workers, relays reply and frame envelopes, sends a CancelEnvelope on socket close, and uses the same envelopes for internal requests to the code-indexing worker (indexing port) and between the indexing workers (summary job execution).

Router publishes clients; the code-indexing worker publishes the index lane and the store slot (repos with completeness, unattributed count) after every change; the summary worker publishes the summary lane and sweep; the admin worker reads snapshot(). s2 delivers the additive publishLane method and its hub binding.

errorCases.scenario: The admin worker exits (uncaught exception, import failure, out of memory).
errorCases.detection: The router's 'exit' listener on the admin Worker fires; its in-flight admin requests are in the router's pending map.
errorCases.response: reclaim(threadId); unregister; answer each in-flight admin request {id, error: "the daemon's admin thread stopped while serving <method>; retry"}; start a replacement; admin requests arriving meanwhile wait for it (at most 30 s). Restarts are rate-limited (5 in 60 s); past the limit the router logs fatal and runs shutdown. s2 supervises the workers it introduces (admin, code-indexing, document-summary); s4 extends the same supervision to session workers and owns the unified view (HLD boundary note 2026-10-22). Every worker the router starts is registered with the lock framework's watchWorker, so a dead worker's maintenance-lock holds are reclaimed; the router reclaims its store-guard permits itself.
errorCases.userImpact: One status call may fail; the next is answered by the new admin worker.

errorCases.detection: Its 'exit' listener fires; its pending indexing requests and internal port requests are in the router's pending map.
errorCases.response: reclaim; fail its pending requests with "the daemon's indexing thread stopped while serving <method>; retry"; tell the summary worker to abandon its current job; start a new code-indexing worker, which restarts the indexer from the persisted registry as a boot does (the interrupted job's file or repo is picked up by the start-up reconcile). The board keeps the last lane state until the new worker publishes.
errorCases.userImpact: An indexing request in flight errors; indexing resumes on its own.

errorCases.detection: Its 'exit' listener fires while the code-indexing worker's remote summary processor awaits a job.
errorCases.response: The router tells the code-indexing worker, whose remote processor rejects that job (logged as 'job failed', as a throwing summary is today) so the summary lane continues; a new summary worker is started before the next summary job is handed over.
errorCases.userImpact: One document's summary is retried on the next sweep, as a failed summary is today.

errorCases.scenario: A worker exits holding the DuckDB permit.
errorCases.detection: reclaim(threadId) reports duckdb in released, or in unhealthy past its quiescence limit.
errorCases.response: reclaim logs and marks; the replacement starts; daemon.status keeps answering.
errorCases.userImpact: db_file tools may fail after an unhealthy reclaim until restart.

errorCases.scenario: The graph store loses its locks.
errorCases.detection: Any thread's recordLocksLost wins the shared health word and broadcasts (s1).
errorCases.response: Unchanged: every thread's next store call fails with LmdbStoreLocksLostError; status answers with storeFailure; shutdown skips the drain and the close and ends by SIGKILL. Maintenance never starts while health is not ok, and an in-progress maintenance stops waiting and takes the same path.

errorCases.scenario: Requests already running do not finish within the pause limit after maintenance asked for the lock.
errorCases.detection: The exclusive lock request's timeoutMs (the pause limit, 10 minutes, config) expires with a LockTimeoutError naming the shared holders.
errorCases.response: Maintenance is abandoned before anything is closed: the exclusive request is withdrawn (new requests are accepted again), a warning names the holders, and the idle check starts over. A manual daemon.compact in this case answers {error: 'daemon.compact: the daemon did not become idle within <limit>; try again later'}.
errorCases.userImpact: Compaction is skipped; nothing is lost and requests are served.

errorCases.response: As today the store is left at its original path (the rename failure path restores .bak); the main thread reopens it, the workers reopen on next use, the maintenance lock is released so requests are accepted again; the failure is logged and returned to a manual daemon.compact caller as today's error message.
errorCases.userImpact: Compaction failed with an error; the daemon keeps serving.

errorCases.scenario: A worker's reply or frame cannot be structured-cloned.
errorCases.detection: postMessage throws DataCloneError in the worker's reply path.
errorCases.response: The worker sends a ReplyEnvelope with error "the result of <method> could not be returned: <message>" (or a stream error frame), so the socket is always answered.
errorCases.userImpact: One request fails with a named error instead of hanging.

errorCases.scenario: The socket closes while its request runs on a worker.
errorCases.detection: IpcServer's socket 'close' listener calls the cancel function from forward().
errorCases.response: For a stream request the router sends a CancelEnvelope and the worker aborts the stream handler's AbortSignal, as today. For a unary request nothing is aborted: the handler runs to completion as today and the router drops its late reply, as today's write to a closed socket does.

errorCases.scenario: A background timer (conversation prune, todo retention) or a watcher-driven write fires during compaction.
errorCases.detection: The timer's run requests the maintenance lock shared with a bounded wait; a store access that slips past it hits getGraphStore's maintenance guard.
errorCases.response: The run waits until maintenance releases the lock (or skips this tick at its bound and logs it); getGraphStore rejects with MaintenanceInProgress rather than reopening the original file before the rename.
errorCases.userImpact: No background write is lost or written to the file being replaced.

edgeCases.input: daemon.status polls arrive every few seconds from the TUI and plugins while the daemon is otherwise idle.
edgeCases.expected: They do not count as activity, so the idle timer still reaches 30 minutes and maintenance can run.

edgeCases.input: A session request arrives during maintenance.
edgeCases.expected: It is refused at once with {error: "daemon busy: compaction since <time> (<reason>); retry later"}; daemon.status meanwhile reports maintenance compacting with the same activity and reason.

edgeCases.input: daemon.compact while the queue has work.
edgeCases.expected: Today's refusal: 'daemon.compact: indexer is busy (queue=N, processing=...)'.

edgeCases.input: The idle timer fires but reclaimable space is below 25% or 256 MB.
edgeCases.expected: No maintenance; the check runs again after the next idle period.

edgeCases.input: daemon.status before the first store publish.
edgeCases.expected: The admin worker waits for the first publish (at most 5 s); past that it reads the registry from the store as today, so repo.list and daemon.status answer exactly today's list.

edgeCases.input: A stream request for a unary-only method.
edgeCases.expected: The serving thread falls back to the unary handler and the client gets one {id, result} line, as today.

edgeCases.input: A step handler on the main thread makes a nested call to repo.reindex.
edgeCases.expected: The in-daemon client routes it to the code-indexing worker and returns its reply; it never runs on the main thread.

edgeCases.input: A file change while a long session request runs on the main thread.
edgeCases.expected: The watcher on the code-indexing worker enqueues and indexes it; the main thread's busy loop does not delay it.

edgeCases.input: A request arrives after maintenance asked for the lock but before the running requests finished.
edgeCases.expected: Refused with the maintenance activity and reason (writer preference), even though compaction has not started yet.

edgeCases.input: An indexing job is due while maintenance holds the lock.
edgeCases.expected: The queue's job loop waits for the lock (it has no caller to refuse) and starts the job once maintenance releases it.

edgeCases.input: A client keeps an understanding.watch or todos.subscribe stream open for hours.
edgeCases.expected: The stream does not keep the daemon from becoming idle and does not block maintenance; refreshes due during maintenance are skipped and resume after it.

migration.stateBefore: One JavaScript thread serves everything: IpcServer (src/daemon/server.ts:79-300) calls handlers[method] directly; main() (src/daemon/index.ts:127-2099) builds the handler tables, starts IndexerService over IndexQueue and Watcher (index.ts:265-302) and wires shutdown (src/daemon/shutdown.ts:115-168). migration.stateAfter: The main thread routes: it keeps the socket, the attached-client registry (published to the board), the board, step state, the target registry, the guard block, LMDB's process-wide open and reader check, the embedding-backend decision, session handlers (until s3), the indexing port, maintenance and shutdown. Admin methods run on the admin worker from the board and daemon.info; indexing methods, IndexQueue, Watcher and IndexerService run on the code-indexing worker; summary jobs execute on the document-summary worker, still started only while code indexing is idle. Compaction runs as idle maintenance holding every request but daemon.status. Wire responses are unchanged; daemon.status gains an optional maintenance field.

migrationSteps.action: Add the frozen method-class table and its coverage test over the constructed handler tables; nothing routes through it yet.

Move handler-table construction from main() into a runtime function taking its indexing dependencies, still called on the main thread with the real queue and indexer, so behaviour is byte-identical and every suite passes.
Give IpcServer the forward seam with today's wire writing and switch every construction site to directDispatch; existing suites pass unchanged.
Add publishLane and its hub binding to the board, the daemon.info hub op, and the admin module reading them, with recorded-response tests against the single-thread answers.
Start the admin worker and route admin methods to it behind daemon.threads.enabled.

Start the code-indexing worker with the queue, watcher and indexer and the document-summary worker executing summary jobs; give the main thread's runtime the indexing port and the in-daemon client its routing; push the embedding backend; publish lanes and the store slot.
Add worker supervision (exit handling, lock reclaim, restart limits) and rewire shutdown to stop the workers, wait for the drain and close the stores on the main thread after they exit.

Add the maintenance controller on the daemon maintenance lock (lock framework afcfa027): every request takes it shared with no wait and is refused with the activity and reason while maintenance holds it; idle detection, the reclaimable estimate, the exclusive request with the pause limit, handle close, compaction and release; route daemon.compact through it, keeping today's responses; register every worker with watchWorker.
Run the contention, routing, indexing-order, maintenance, restart and smoke tests; then default daemon.threads.enabled on and release with the installer (clients need no update).

migration.backwardCompat: The IPC contract is unchanged: socket path and permissions, method names, request shapes and every response field and meaning, including 'unknown method', 'invalid JSON', stream framing, the stream-to-unary fallback, the named LmdbStoreLocksLostError message, and daemon.compact's result and busy refusal. daemon.status gains one optional field (maintenance) present only while compaction runs. The only behavioural change clients see is that during idle maintenance their requests other than daemon.status are refused with the maintenance activity and reason and must be retried. With daemon.threads.enabled off the daemon runs single-threaded as today.

alternativesConsidered.name: Whole queue on the code-indexing worker; the document-summary worker executes summary jobs
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: IndexQueue keeps both lanes, their ordering and the summary yield unchanged on the code-indexing worker; its summary lane's processor sends each summary job to the document-summary worker and awaits it, so lane semantics are today's by construction.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Common to every alternative: a frozen sc5 class table (src/daemon/threads/method-class.ts) with a coverage test over the runtime handler tables; a router on the main thread wrapping IpcServer with a forward seam (unknown-method check in the router), the attached-client registry published to the board, and request holding during maintenance; an admin worker running a small admin module (daemon.status, debug-status, repo.list, config.show/catalog, guide.list/get, shutdown/update via a router hub op) reading the board and a daemon.info router hub op; session handlers still on the main thread with an indexing port in place of the local queue/indexer objects (board-backed sync reads for depth and lanes, internal requests to the code-indexing worker for codeIndexWorkFor, depthForRepo, enqueue, addRepo/removeRepo); the in-daemon client sending non-session methods through the router; maintenance compaction run by the main thread. Specific to a1: the code-indexing worker hosts IndexQueue, Watcher and IndexerService exactly as main() does today and serves every indexing-class method. The summary lane's drain loop stays in that IndexQueue, with its yield to the index lane unchanged; its processor, for a summary job, sends the job to the document-summary worker over a dedicated channel and awaits completion. The document-summary worker runs IndexerService's summary paths (docSummariseRepo, docSummariseEntity) against its own store handles; their queue reads (isIndexIdle, isStopping) come from two words in a shared block the code-indexing worker writes, waitForIndexIdle waits on that word, and takeDocSummaryEdit is a request back to the code-indexing worker. Each worker publishes its own lane (publishLane) and sweep progress to the board.
pros: The lane ordering, the summary yield and stop/drain stay in the one existing IndexQueue, so ac6's 'same order and results as today' holds by construction
The model-heavy summary work runs off the code-indexing thread, so code indexing never waits on a summary's CPU or I/O
Smallest change to queue.ts and indexer code: a remote processor for one lane plus shared-word reads for the sweep
cons: A summary job runs on another thread while its lane state lives on the code worker, so the code worker's event loop must stay responsive to forward and complete jobs (it is, apart from synchronous indexing steps)
takeDocSummaryEdit becomes a cross-thread request inside the sweep

alternativesConsidered.name: Split lanes: each indexing worker owns its lane, coordinated through a shared code-busy word
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: IndexQueue is split: the code-indexing worker owns the index lane, the document-summary worker owns the summary lane and the sweep; summary jobs enqueued on the code side are forwarded to the summary worker, and the yield reads a shared code-busy word.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Common parts as in a1. IndexQueue gains a per-thread lane set: on the code-indexing worker only the index lane runs and a summary job passed to enqueue is forwarded (through the router) to the document-summary worker; on the document-summary worker only the summary lane runs, and isIndexIdle / waitForIndexIdle read and wait on a shared code-busy word (index lane in flight or queued) that the code worker updates. depth, laneStatus and depthForRepo are composed from both workers' board lanes; takeDocSummaryEdit is local to the summary worker.
pros: Each worker is self-contained: the summary sweep, its edits and its lane live together
No job forwarding per summary execution, only per enqueue
cons: The queue's ordering logic is duplicated across two partial queues; depth, depthForRepo and codeIndexWorkFor must be recomposed from two places, so equality with today's ordering is a property to re-prove rather than inherit
A summary enqueued during the forward hop is invisible to either side's depth for that moment, so status can briefly under-count
Larger change to queue.ts semantics and its tests
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Self-contained workers, but ac6, ac7 and k7 are only partial because the queue's ordering is split and recomposed.

alternativesConsidered.name: Both lanes on one indexing worker (no second thread)
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: One indexing worker hosts today's queue with both lanes; no document-summary thread.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Common parts as in a1, but a single indexing worker runs IndexQueue with both lanes and IndexerService unchanged, as the original HLD's single indexing thread did.
pros: Smallest change: the queue and indexer move unchanged onto one worker
cons: Violates k3 as amended (code indexing and document summaries on two threads): a summary's synchronous work still delays code indexing on the same thread
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Violates ac6 and the stakeholder's two-thread decision.

openQuestions: Pause-acknowledgement limit for maintenance (default 10 minutes) and the maintenance thresholds (30 min idle, 25% and 256 MB reclaimable) are config values; confirm the defaults after the first live runs.

Supervision boundary: s2 supervises the workers it introduces (exit handling, lock reclaim, replacement, restart limit) so no s2 worker crash leaves the daemon broken until s4; s4 extends it to every worker class. Recorded as an HLD boundary note on 2026-10-22.

Depends on the lock framework (standalone Story afcfa027, LLD approved 2026-10-22); s2's build starts after that Story's build. Session workers (s3) need no pause registry: they take the maintenance lock shared per request and are registered with watchWorker.
